title: Results after breast-conserving surgery and the adjuvant plan

brief.setting: Breast clinic, two weeks after surgery
brief.scenario: Ms Rachel Linford, 42, had a left wide local excision and sentinel lymph node biopsy. Histology: 19 mm invasive carcinoma (no special type, grade 2), ER positive, HER2 negative; all margins clear (nearest 2 mm); 0 of 2 sentinel nodes involved. A genomic test showed a low recurrence risk. The MDT recommends no further surgery and no chemotherapy, whole-breast radiotherapy, and endocrine therapy (probably tamoxifen), to be finalised with the oncologist.
brief.task: Explain the results and the plan to Ms Linford.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Headline first, then what it means, then why radiotherapy and tablets still matter.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Letting "clear" sound like "cured, no more treatment".
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "The results are good news. Can I go through them?"

grid.label: Opening and headline
grid.fail: Buries the result under a description of the laboratory process.
grid.pass: Asks about her recovery and wound, then gives the headline early: good news, the cancer was fully removed and nodes clear.
grid.high: Checks she is ready and who she would like present before giving results.

grid.label: Explaining the results
grid.fail: Says "it's clear" without explaining, or implies she is cured.
grid.pass: Clear margins mean no further operation; nodes free of cancer mean no more armpit surgery.
grid.high: Explains the genomic test: low risk, so chemotherapy would add too little benefit to recommend.

grid.label: Radiotherapy
grid.fail: Cannot say why radiotherapy is still needed after clear results.
grid.pass: Radiotherapy to the breast roughly halves the chance of the cancer coming back there; five daily treatments over one week.
grid.high: Mentions tiredness and skin redness, and a breath-hold technique to protect the heart as the cancer is left-sided.

grid.label: Endocrine therapy
grid.fail: Omits the tablets, or says a "few months".
grid.pass: Hormone-sensitive cancer: a daily tablet, probably tamoxifen, for at least 5 years lowers the risk of return.
grid.high: Explains the oncologist will discuss tamoxifen alone or with ovarian suppression, and that treatment may extend beyond 5 years.

grid.label: Her concern about side effects
grid.fail: Dismisses her worry as "standard" or tells her she must take them.
grid.pass: Asks what she has heard, acknowledges hot flushes, and says they can be managed.
grid.high: Adds: report unusual vaginal bleeding or leg swelling, use non-hormonal contraception, and never stop without discussing.

grid.label: Continuity of care
grid.pass: Oncology referral for radiotherapy planning and endocrine therapy; breast care nurse remains her named contact.
grid.high: Gives written information, and mentions follow-up with mammography.

grid.label: Understanding and closing
grid.pass: Asks her to summarise, invites questions, closes clearly.
grid.high: Answers "Am I cured?" honestly: very reassuring results, treatment keeps recurrence risk as low as possible.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel. Can I check your name and date of birth? How's the wound? I have your results, and it's good news: the cancer was removed completely and the lymph nodes were clear.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Clear edges mean you don't need another operation. No cancer in the nodes means no more surgery under the arm.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Radiotherapy roughly halves the chance of the cancer coming back. It's five daily treatments over one week.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Your cancer is hormone-sensitive, so a daily tablet, probably tamoxifen, for at least 5 years lowers the risk of it returning.

pass.speaker: examiner

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: What did she go through? Hot flushes do happen, and there are ways to manage them.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'll refer you to the oncologist, and Sarah stays your contact.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Can you tell me what you're taking away today? Any questions?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel. Can I check your name and date of birth? How's the wound? Would you like anyone with you before we go through the results?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It's good news. The cancer was removed completely, with clear edges, so no further operation. The two nodes were clear, so no more surgery under the arm. A genomic test showed a low risk, so chemotherapy would add too little to recommend.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Two more things. Radiotherapy roughly halves the chance of it coming back: five daily treatments over one week. Tiredness and skin redness are usual, and as it's the left side, you'll hold your breath during treatment to protect the heart.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It's hormone-sensitive, so a daily tablet for at least 5 years, maybe longer. The oncologist will discuss tamoxifen alone, or with treatment to switch off the ovaries.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Ms Linford: “My sister had awful hot flushes on those.”

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: What did she go through? Flushes can be managed. Tell us about unusual vaginal bleeding or a swollen leg, use non-hormonal contraception, and please don't stop without talking to us.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'll refer you to the oncologist; Sarah stays your named contact. Here's written information; you'll have regular mammograms.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: These results are very reassuring, and the treatment keeps the risk of it coming back as low as possible. What will you tell your husband tonight?

failures.move: Describing the laboratory process before the result.
failures.consequence: Prolongs her anxiety; she hears nothing until she knows whether it is good or bad.
False reassurance that makes radiotherapy and tablets seem pointless.
Without a reason, she may decline radiotherapy that roughly halves recurrence.
A known reason women stop tamoxifen early, left unexplored and unmanaged.

recovery.line: Let me start with the most important part: it's good news.
Clear means the operation worked; radiotherapy and tablets lower the risk further.

knowledge.fact: Invasive cancer: further surgery for tumour on ink (0 mm); consider it within 1 mm. A 2 mm margin is clear.
Node-negative women: radiotherapy after conservation cut 10-year recurrence from 31% to 16%.
Five years of tamoxifen roughly halves recurrence in ER-positive disease during treatment and cuts breast cancer death by about a third.
Premenopausal: tamoxifen alone, or ovarian suppression with tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor, by shared decision.
Tamoxifen: hot flushes, thromboembolism, endometrial changes; avoid pregnancy, use non-hormonal contraception.

recall.think: "Clear" is not "cured"; she may skip treatment she does not understand.
recall.say: "It's good news: fully removed, nodes clear."
recall.trap: Treating clear results as the end of treatment.
recall.finish: Oncology referral; nurse remains her contact.

sources.name: NICE NG101: Early and locally advanced breast cancer: diagnosis and management
sources.version: Published 18 July 2018; last updated 14 April 2025 (links updated July 2026)
sources.supports: Named clinical nurse specialist (1.1.1); further surgery only for tumour on ink (0 mm), considered for invasive cancer within 1 mm (1.4.3, 1.4.5); no further axillary treatment when sentinel nodes are negative; systemic therapy decisions by the MDT with the person (1.6.2); adjuvant endocrine therapy for ER-positive disease (1.11.5); premenopausal women: shared decision between tamoxifen alone and ovarian function suppression with tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor (1.11.6); consider tamoxifen beyond 5 years (1.11.16); breath-hold technique for left-sided cancer (1.13.2); whole-breast radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery with clear margins (1.13.3); 26 Gy in 5 fractions over 1 week (1.13.13)

sources.name: NICE DG58: Tumour profiling tests to guide adjuvant chemotherapy decisions in early breast cancer
sources.supports: Oncotype DX, EndoPredict and Prosigna as options to guide adjuvant chemotherapy decisions in ER-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative early breast cancer

sources.name: Early Breast Cancer Trialists' Collaborative Group (Darby S, et al.). Effect of radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery on 10-year recurrence and 15-year breast cancer death. Lancet 2011;378:1707-1716
sources.supports: In node-negative women, radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery reduced the 10-year risk of any first recurrence from 31.0% to 15.6%, and reduced 15-year breast cancer death

sources.name: Early Breast Cancer Trialists' Collaborative Group (Davies C, et al.). Relevance of breast cancer hormone receptors and other factors to the efficacy of adjuvant tamoxifen. Lancet 2011;378:771-784
sources.supports: In ER-positive disease, about 5 years of tamoxifen roughly halved recurrence in years 0-4 (RR 0.53) and reduced breast cancer mortality by about a third over 15 years

sources.name: Tamoxifen 10 mg film-coated tablets: Summary of Product Characteristics (Wockhardt UK Ltd)
sources.version: Date of revision of the text 14 May 2026
sources.supports: Hot flushes and thromboembolic events are recognised adverse effects; endometrial changes, so abnormal vaginal bleeding must be investigated; avoid pregnancy and use barrier or other non-hormonal contraception

sources.name: GMC: Good medical practice
sources.supports: Give patients the information they want or need in a way they can understand; be honest; support patients to make decisions

partner.opening: Ms Linford is here for her results. Please begin when you're ready.
partner.actorBrief: You are Rachel Linford, 42, a primary school teacher with two children aged 8 and 11, two weeks after surgery to your left breast. Your wound has healed well. You have dreaded this appointment. Opening: "Is it good or bad?" If given the good news early, relax and engage. If told it is "clear", ask "So I'm done?" Hidden concern: your sister had bad hot flushes on hormone tablets and stopped them; say "My sister had awful hot flushes on those" once, and only say she stopped them if asked. Ask "Am I cured?" near the end. If asked to summarise, say: "It's all out, glands clear, a week of radiotherapy, then tablets for years."

reveals.finding: "The wound's fine. A bit numb under the arm."
"Flushes all night, no sleep. She stopped them after a year."

reveals.trigger: Asks whether she could be pregnant or plans a pregnancy
reveals.finding: "No, we're done. I'm on the pill, though."

push.question: Why do I need radiotherapy if it's all out?
push.expect: Microscopic disease may remain in the breast; radiotherapy roughly halves the risk of return.

push.question: How long will I take the tablets?
push.expect: At least 5 years, possibly longer; the choice of tablet made with the oncologist.

curveballs.prompt: "I'm on the combined pill. Is that OK?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Hormonal contraception is not advised with hormone-sensitive breast cancer; switch to a non-hormonal method such as a copper coil, discussed with the oncologist or GP.
It is her choice; explain the benefit, and ask her to discuss side effects with oncology before deciding.

curveballs.prompt: "Why no chemotherapy? My friend had it."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Her tumour's genomic test showed low risk, so chemotherapy would add little benefit for its side effects.
